title: Optical switching of antiferromagnetic domains by nonreciprocal heat current
authors: Takeshi Hayashida, Shunsuke Izumikawa, Kenta Kimura, Carl S. Davies, Andrei Kirilyuk
abstract: What distinguishes front from back? In physics, such directionality emerges only when an underlying symmetry is broken. Antiferromagnets that inherently break both space-inversion and time-reversal symmetries provide a striking example, exhibiting nonreciprocal optical responses that depend on the direction of light propagation. Beyond distinguishing antiferromagnetic domains, we show that this nonreciprocity can deterministically create them. Using mid-infrared light, we demonstrate deterministic switching of antiferromagnetic domains in the magnetoelectric antiferromagnet LiFePO4, where illumination from opposite sides selectively stabilizes opposite domain states. Remarkably, the switching persists over a broad wavelength range rather than being confined to a narrow transition-specific spectral region, overcoming the spectral and material constraints of resonance-based optical switching schemes. The broadband switching originates from the material's intrinsic nonreciprocity through optically generated heat currents. Our results establish nonreciprocity as a general principle for deterministically controlling symmetry-broken phases with light.
summary: The researchers demonstrated the deterministic switching of antiferromagnetic domains in LiFePO4 using mid-infrared light. They established that this nonreciprocal switching mechanism is governed by optically-generated heat currents, proving a general principle for controlling symmetry-broken phases with light. This overcomes limitations found in resonance-based optical control methods.
main_problem: To determine if nonreciprocity itself, rather than resonance enhancement, can provide a general principle for deterministically controlling symmetry-broken phases using light.
main_result: Deterministic, nonreciprocal switching of antiferromagnetic domains is achieved using mid-IR light, mediated by optically-generated heat currents.
method: Domain imaging and time-resolved measurements were performed using mid-infrared pulses from a Free-Electron Laser facility (FELIX).
model_or_system: The study uses the magnetoelectric antiferromagnet LiFePO4, which inherently breaks both space-inversion and time-reversal symmetries. The control mechanism is attributed to nonreciprocal heat currents generated by directional light propagation.
key_observables: Domain states (L+ and L-), direction-dependent switching efficiency, transient changes in transmitted light intensity, and the magnitude of the optically-generated heat current.
important_parameters: Mid-infrared wavelength range ($7–19\ \mu	ext{m}$), low temperature ($4\ 	ext{K}$), and the comparison between front-side vs. back-side pumping directions.
main_assumptions: The switching mechanism is primarily governed by nonreciprocal heat currents, overcoming spectral constraints associated with resonance-based schemes. The conclusion regarding NDD absence is limited by experimental sensitivity.
figures_summary: Figures demonstrate domain structure via NDD imaging and show that front-side pumping induces L+ to L- switching while back-side pumping reverses this. Time-resolved data track the transient changes associated with heating and switching.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical basis (symmetry breaking in AFMs), demonstrates nonreciprocal domain switching using mid-IR light, attributes the mechanism to directional heat currents, and rules out simple resonant dichroism as the sole cause.
why_interesting: This work provides an experimental demonstration of controlling symmetry-broken quantum phases using fundamental directional properties (nonreciprocity) rather than relying on specific material resonances, which is highly relevant for designing general optical control schemes in condensed matter systems.
